extracted.intended_audience: beginner-to-intermediate TeX users / authors preparing plain-TeX manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and evaluative guidance for running plain TeX, diagnosing typesetting problems (overfull/underfull boxes, badness, hyphenation), and handling TeX error interaction and tokenization issues. Focused on producing acceptable typeset output and interpreting TeX's diagnostic messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Input line and paragraph rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A return is like a space; two spaces count as one; a blank line denotes the end of a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may type long or short source lines arbitrarily; TeX treats input lines independently of output lines, so break source lines where convenient for editing. Remember that a blank line (two returns) ends a paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of % for comments and line termination
rubrics_metrics.description: The '%' sign terminates the remainder of the input line; TeX ignores everything following '%' up to the end of that line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '%' to insert comments into your manuscript without introducing the normal inter-word space that an end-of-line would insert. Also use '%' to prevent unwanted spaces at line ends (e.g., when splitting lines in source). Plain TeX sets '%' as the comment character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonbreaking tie (~) and special accent commands
rubrics_metrics.description: The tie character (~) is treated as a normal space but prevents line breaking at that point; accent commands like \" (umlaut) and \c (cedilla) produce accented characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ties within multi-word names or phrases to avoid line breaks in undesirable places. Examples: \"o for an umlauted o; \c produces a cedilla. See Chapter 14 for more on ties and breaking rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved characters in plain TeX and escaping them
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain characters are reserved by the format (e.g., \ { } $ & # ^ _ % ~) and cannot be used ordinarily; escape them with a backslash when you need the literal symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sequences like \$ \% \& \# \_ \{ \} and \backslash to obtain the literal characters in text or math. Remember the format reserves category codes for special purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to invoke TeX and format preloading
rubrics_metrics.description: At the initial prompt ('**') TeX will insert \input if the first character typed is not a backslash; an ampersand before the name (e.g., '&plain') tells TeX to replace its memory with a precomputed format file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can run TeX interactively by typing the filename (TeX supplies the '.tex' suffix). Shortcuts like 'tex story' may exist on some systems. Use '&plain story' or ':&plain story' to load the plain format explicitly if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overfull \hbox reporting and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX reports 'Overfull \hbox (Xpt too wide) in paragraph at lines m--n' and prints an abbreviated form of the offending box contents along with how much it sticks out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat overfull boxes as visual errors (TeX inserts a black rule) and use the log file or on-screen messages to locate the offending paragraph and measure how much it exceeds the box. Overfull messages show the paragraph lines and the abbreviated box contents (with '[]' standing for indentation or complex constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Badness metric and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX assigns a numerical 'badness' to each line reflecting spacing quality: 0 perfect, 12 somewhat loose/tight, 100 tight, 200 loose (plain TeX normally disallows badness >200), up to extreme values (1000 bad, 5000 awful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the mapping of numeric badness to qualitative spacing. Plain TeX normally stipulates no line badness should exceed 200; if your layout forces higher badness (e.g., very narrow columns), adjust tolerance or rewrite text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance (\tolerance) vs. diagnosing spacing problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The \tolerance parameter controls the maximum line badness TeX will accept before producing overfull boxes; setting it higher allows wider spacing and suppresses overfull boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use high \tolerance (e.g., 1600) to avoid overfull boxes when columns are narrow, or use \tolerance=10000 to treat tolerance as infinite (never produce overfull boxes except for words wider than the column). For diagnosis, you may prefer lower tolerance so overfull boxes indicate where to fix text; for quick checks, higher tolerance is convenient but may hide problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: \hbadness and underfull/underfull reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: \hbadness sets the threshold above which TeX reports underfull/overly bad lines; plain TeX sets \hbadness=1000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set \hbadness to a desired threshold (e.g., 500) to suppress messages for less-severe badness while still reporting the truly serious lines. Combine with \tolerance to control reporting vs. enforcement behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: \hfuzz to ignore small overfulls
rubrics_metrics.description: \hfuzz specifies a tolerance (in points) under which an overfull box is ignored (not considered erroneous); plain TeX sets \hfuzz=0.0pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set \hfuzz=1pt (or similar) to avoid worrying about tiny protrusions; useful when slight overfulls are visually acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation remedies and hints
rubrics_metrics.description: When overfulls are due to hyphenation limits, give TeX hyphenation hints either by inserting discretionary hyphens (e.g., 'gal\-axy') or by declaring \hyphenation{gal-axy} near the start of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try discretionary hyphens in problem words or a global \hyphenation list to improve break points. Appendix H describes the hyphenation algorithm in detail. If hyphenation exhausted all options, consider other remedies (tolerance, rewriting, column width).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative spacing strategies (\raggedright and ragged settings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \raggedright to allow ragged-right setting so TeX does not try to keep the right margin uniform; then badness reflects the amount of right-margin space rather than inter-word spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very narrow columns, \raggedright often produces better-looking text by avoiding extreme stretching of inter-word spaces. Combine with reduced \hsize and appropriate \tolerance as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs: inspect overfull boxes vs. suppress warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Two strategies: (A) set a high tolerance and low reporting threshold (	olerance high, \hbadness set) to learn 'how bad it is' without overfull boxes, or (B) set a stricter tolerance so overfull boxes appear, making it clearer what corrective actions are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option A is useful when you don't have time to fix spacing but want a sense of severity; Option B is better when you want concrete visual evidence (overfull black bars) to guide repairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and using the transcript/log file
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX always writes a transcript/log file (.log) recording messages (including overfull/underfull details and internal hbox/glue/kern listings) so you can inspect messages after they scroll by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine story.log and texput.log to retrieve overfull messages and the detailed internals TeX reports; the log contains the abbreviated box contents and numeric amounts that help diagnose spacing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting multi-line error context
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX prints error contexts in pairs of lines; the top line shows what TeX has just read and the next what it is about to read; nested contexts show macro expansion levels (e.g., '#1->\line{\hss #1 \hss}').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering multiline errors (e.g., undefined control sequence inside a macro expansion), inspect the bottom line (what you typed) and the top line (what triggered the error) for clues. Use the context to trace through macro expansion to find the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX interactive error options and recommended practice
rubrics_metrics.description: At the '?' prompt TeX accepts several responses: <return> to proceed, s to scroll future messages, R to run without stopping, Q to run quietly, I to insert text, E to edit the file, a number to delete tokens, w or h for help, x to quit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'w' to get the informal help message explaining the error and suggesting recovery strategies. Use 'E' to terminate and edit the source if you want to fix the file; use 's' or 'R' for noninteractive runs where you still want messages to be recorded in the log. Prefer detecting and fixing errors during runs to increase productivity and reduce reruns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling interaction mode via primitives
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX primitives \scrollmode, \nonstopmode, \batchmode correspond to typing s, R, Q respectively in response to an error; \errorstopmode restores normal interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place these primitives in your file to control the interaction level programmatically (they are global). Many installations also allow keyboard interruption that reverts to \errorstopmode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \errorcontextlines to adjust macro context verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: \errorcontextlines controls how many two-line context items TeX prints in error messages (plain TeX sets it to 5); setting it to 0 reduces verbosity, larger values increase context shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If macro-expanded error messages are inscrutable, increase \errorcontextlines (e.g., to 100) for debugging; set to 0 to suppress most context in routine runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tokenization rules: tokens vs characters and permanence of category codes
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX converts input into tokens: either a character with an attached category code or a control sequence. Once a character token is made its category code is permanent; control sequences are single tokens whose meaning is looked up when processed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know that spaces after control words are discarded during tokenization, and that changing category codes later does not affect characters already tokenized. Understanding tokens is essential for grasping TeX macro behavior and debugging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control-sequence arguments and macro expansion behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Macros that take arguments (e.g., \centerline) save their argument tokens and later expand them where placeholders (e.g., #1) occur; errors inside such arguments produce multiline contexts showing expansion stack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an undefined control sequence appears inside an argument, TeX may not complain until expansion time. Use the displayed expansion context to find where the undefined control sequence arose and correct the input (or edit at the spot using 'E').

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical experimental approach to learning TeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn by running directed experiments: change \hsize, \tolerance, \hfuzz, use \raggedright, insert discretionary hyphens, and observe overfull/underfull behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual's experiments (changing column widths and tolerances) are recommended to gain a practical feel for TeX's line-breaking and error-reporting mechanisms. Use the log and overfull markers to inform corrections.
